overview: This file documents three aspects of Japan’s industrial capacity and recovery during the Allied occupation. An October 1946 memorandum estimates Japan’s surviving machine-tool inventory, productive capacity, and equipment potentially available for reparations; a May 1949 Army telegram supplies production and consumption statistics for copper, lead, zinc, and aluminum; and an August 1949 despatch and its enclosures investigate the wartime manufacture and possible postwar revival of tetraethyl lead. The latter correspondence records bombing damage, conversion of chemical plants to dyestuff production, the disposition of specialized equipment, patent concerns raised on behalf of a British company, and a detailed Japanese description of the manufacturing process.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Japanese machine-tool industry and inventories
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s surviving machine-tool inventory, productive capacity, and the number of tools and plants potentially available for reparations.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum estimates Japan’s 1944 machine-tool holdings at 788,700 units and its post-bombing inventory at approximately 600,000, while cautioning that the definition and condition of the equipment make the figure uncertain. It places peak annual productive capacity at about 67,000 units and notes that the Interim Program would reduce it to 27,000, potentially freeing capacity for 40,000 units annually. It further estimates that roughly 200,000 existing tools could become available for reparations from the machine-tool industry, arsenals, aircraft factories, munitions plants, and other facilities. Limited postwar production was apparently serving mining, food-processing, textile, and other civilian industries.

subfiles.title: Army telegram reporting Japanese nonferrous-metal statistics
subfiles.about: Reports actual 1948 and estimated 1949 production and consumption figures for copper, lead, zinc, and aluminum in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram provides metric-ton statistics for mined or concentrated metal content, primary refined output, scrap, and consumption of copper, lead, zinc, and aluminum. It compares actual 1948 results with 1949 estimates, although several scrap figures were unavailable. The document explains that the 1948 consumption figures represent shipments made against allocation tickets.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 532 transmitting correspondence on tetraethyl lead
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits three memoranda concerning Japan’s wartime and prospective postwar manufacture of tetraethyl lead.
subfiles.summary: The Political Adviser forwards an Australian inquiry, SCAP’s response, and a Nippon Soda memorandum describing the manufacturing process. The covering despatch suggests that this information about a lesser-known Japanese industry may interest several United States government agencies. Copies were also directed to the American embassies in Canberra and London.

subfiles.title: Australian Mission inquiry about resuming tetraethyl-lead manufacture
subfiles.from: Patrick Shaw, Head of the Australian Mission in Japan
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, attention G-2 Foreign Liaison
subfiles.about: Requests information about possible renewed Japanese manufacture of tetraethyl lead and associated intermediates, with particular concern for foreign patent rights.
subfiles.summary: Acting for the Australian Government and the Far Eastern representative of Associated Ethyl Co. Ltd., Patrick Shaw asks about the potential resumption of tetraethyl-lead manufacture in Japan. He notes that several prewar plants reportedly produced the compound and its intermediates but were damaged or destroyed by bombing. The inquiry seeks assurance that any reconstructed industry would respect patents belonging to British and other foreign owners.

subfiles.title: SCAP report on Japanese tetraethyl-lead plants and patents
subfiles.from: Harry C. Kelly, Acting Chief, Scientific and Technical Division, Economic and Scientific Section, SCAP
subfiles.to: Head of the Australian Mission in Japan
subfiles.about: Identifies Japanese wartime tetraethyl-lead producers and explains the condition, conversion, or destruction of their plants and the status of relevant patents.
subfiles.summary: SCAP identifies facilities operated by Nippon Soda, Hodagaya Chemical, the Second and Third Naval Fuel Depots, and a Mitsui Chemical plant that was nearly ready to begin production when the war ended. Nippon Soda and Mitsui had converted their plants to dyestuff production, while the Hodagaya and naval facilities had been severely damaged by air raids; none of the companies reportedly intended to resume tetraethyl-lead production. The memorandum records past output, including Nippon Soda’s stock of twenty-two kiloliters, and notes that the naval depots were held for reparations. It also discusses Japanese patents 157135 and 167709, formerly made secret at the Japanese Navy’s request, and observes that Associated Ethyl could challenge their validity if its processes anticipated them.

subfiles.title: Nippon Soda description of the tetraethyl-lead manufacturing process
subfiles.about: Describes the successive chemical and mechanical operations used to manufacture tetraethyl lead and formulate ethyl fluid.
subfiles.summary: Nippon Soda explains its preparation of lead-sodium alloy and ethyl chloride, followed by their controlled reaction and steam distillation to obtain tetraethyl lead. It describes a continuous process for recovering waste lead and a separate synthesis of ethylene dibromide from ethylene gas and bromine. The final section gives the percentage formula for ethyl fluid: 64.5 percent tetraethyl lead, 33.7 percent ethylene dibromide, and small quantities of hydro-benzene, dimethyl aniline, Sudan Blue, and light oil.

interest: The file is valuable because it links broad occupation-era policy—industrial demilitarization, reparations, resource allocation, and economic recovery—to unusually specific evidence about individual plants and production processes. Its tetraethyl-lead papers preserve plant-level accounts of bombing damage, postwar conversion to dyestuffs, dormant equipment, naval secrecy, and international patent concerns. The detailed Nippon Soda process and fluid formula are especially distinctive technical evidence, while the machine-tool and metals documents provide quantitative context for Japan’s wider industrial condition after the war.
